newsitem.title: USA: Developing world to show off stability at IMF meet.
newsitem.headline: Developing world to show off stability at IMF meet.

text.p: As the world's economic policymakers gather here this week, emerging markets will be basking in newfound stability after last year's state of crisis, analysts said.

"There is not going to be the gloom and doom of last year when everyone was still shocked about Mexico," said Paulo Leme, director of emerging markets economics at Goldman, Sachs & Co. "The theme will be that a lot of the structural reforms and adjustments are deeper than that one-time crisis."

The annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank will likely focus on how the developing world has blossomed since last year's international package to salvage the Mexican economy.

The emerging markets have fully recovered from the grim days of the "Tequila crisis," when Mexico botched a currency devaluation prompting international investors to flee from assets across the developing world, analysts said.

Indicative of this year's improved climate has been the ability of Mexico and the Philippines to swap its Brady bonds for longer-dated, uncollaterized paper, and the capacity of other nations, such as Peru, to buy back debt from the market.
Another theme likely to arise at the IMF/World Bank meetings will be how the recent rise in oil prices has fuelled prospects for emerging oil exporters such as Venezuela, Mexico, Ecuador and Nigeria.

Although little monumental news was expected to emerge at the annual meetings, emerging markets analysts predicted incremental developments as various nations showed off their healthy economic fundamentals.

Joyce Chang, managing director at Merrill Lynch, said Peru and the IMF would probably finalise the country's Brady bond restructuring, bringing to a close the era of debt refinancing accords left over from the 1980s.
"There will be a theme that this signals the end of the Brady restructuring," Chang said.
Brady bonds, which were named for former U.S. Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady, were issued by emerging market debtors starting in 1990 to replace defaulted commercial bank borrowings.

The IMF might use the meeting to release a second $115 million tranche of standby loan to Bulgaria, which the Fund postponed until the government fulfilled pledges to close loss-making state firms, said Luis R. Luis, head of emerging market research Scudder, Stevens and Clark.
"The resumption of the standby loan is being negotiating continuously," Luis said.
The IMF board might also consider Argentina's Extended Loan Facility, but analysts suggested the final approval might be delayed until after the meetings.

Russia will display its increased economic stability, despite health concerns over President Boris Yeltsin, and analysts said Moscow may clarify the timing of their Eurobond expected in October or November.
Overall, prospects have improved for emerging markets, with strong economic balances and a flood of investment from the industrialised world.
"At this stage things are more balanced than they have been in while," Luis said. "There are no major crises brewing."
